declarations.documentation:
Plug an MCP server's tools into a program for the extent of @continuation@ — the `use mcp.provide(url = ..., auth = ...)` form. The runtime lists the server, hands @continuation@ a `toolbox[Scope]` of one runtime-minted agent per tool (each carrying the server signature — for `reflection.get_metadata` and call-site validation — and the descriptor it was listed with), and settles with the continuation's result. `Scope` rides the continuation's row and is discharged from `provide`'s own, so a tool is callable exactly inside the block; discharging it is `provide`'s alone (only it opens the connection), so a live tool context cannot be forged. Pass the marker explicitly as the first `[...]` argument (`mcp.provide[mcp.scope](...)`), and the toolbox binder's annotation agrees with it.

A missing or dead `oauth` credential pauses on an authorization escalation and retries once answered; rejected `headers` material throws `auth_error`, and a rejected listing throws `server_error`. A tool called after the scope closes is rejected as a typed `server_error`.

Two connections sharing one marker share a scope, so their tools become mutually substitutable in a row carrying it — a type-level distinction only, since routing follows each tool value's own `{url, auth}` descriptor. A marker per connection keeps them apart, which a `katari mcp pull` binding does automatically. When the toolbox is never read, `open` is the listing-free form of this same contract.

Publish @tools@ as a live MCP server for the extent of @subscriber@. The runtime mints a fresh,
unguessable capability URL and serves the record's agents there — each record key is the published tool
name, each agent's declared signature the tool's advertised schema. The URL is the key: possession
grants access, and nothing else does. @subscriber@ receives the URL, hands it to whoever should
connect, and stays alive while calls should be served; when it returns (or the run is cancelled) the
URL deactivates and its result becomes `serve`'s result.

A served agent is self-contained: its effects are handled, or are at most `io` and this module's
throws. A served tool that throws or panics with no handler of its own cancels the whole endpoint, its
failure proxying up and failing the run unless caught above @subscriber@; a handler around a tool's
body turns that into a per-request outcome.

Resolve a usable OAuth bearer token for the stored credential @name@, as a private string — it may
flow only to a submission sink such as an http `Authorization` header, never to a user-facing boundary.
When @name@ has no usable token (never authorized, or refresh-dead) the run pauses on a
`prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation and resumes once the credential is established; a transient
resolution failure throws `server_error`.

its recorded expiry holds (with a ~60s refresh margin) and refreshes once due, so the runtime owns the
caching. That recorded expiry is the only input, so a token revoked before it expires keeps being
served and the API answers 401 / 403 for up to one access-token lifetime; converting that downstream
failure into a `supervise.interrupted` recovers, since each re-run asks afresh.

declarations.documentation:
Dedup by a monotone floor in the source's own receive clock — for a source that can be listed from an
instant ("mail that arrived after T"). The cursor advances to each delivered item's own @mark@, never
on the poller's clock and never past the tick that observed it, so neither a slow tick nor a
future-dated item moves it beyond what has been delivered. The memory alongside it is the keys at or
above the floor, so it stays constant-size however long the subscription runs.

@overlap@ is how far below the floor each fetch re-lists, in the same milliseconds — slack for a source
whose listing boundary is rounded or exclusive (Gmail's `after:` takes whole seconds, so `overlap =
1000` covers both readings). It costs no duplicates, since the keys inside it are the ones still
remembered; 0 fits an exact boundary.

declarations.documentation:
Poll a source on @schedule@ and deliver each item it has not seen before to @deliver_to@, forever —
the durable-subscription skeleton a source package composes instead of rewriting. Shaped like
`time.watch` (`-> never`, @deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged), so it
composes under `parallel [ … ]` beside any other daemon.

Delivery is at-least-once: the commit lands after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in between
re-delivers exactly that item on the next tick. Exactly-once is built at the destination by making the
delivery idempotent, keyed by `item.key`.

@fetch@ is the whole adapter, and its contract is: given @since@ (the instant this tick lists from — the
cursor's floor minus the regime's overlap) and @tick@ (the occurrence's scheduled instant), return every
item at or above @since@, oldest first, across every page of the source's pagination. The order is load-bearing —
the cursor then only passes items that were delivered — and so is draining every page, since a listing
cut off at a newest-first cap leaves the older items below the cursor. Returning an item again is free;
that is what the remembered keys are for.

With `skip_backlog` it reports arrivals: whatever the source already held is not delivered however well
it matches, and an old item that comes to match later is not delivered either (the fetch does not look
below the cursor). With `continuity = resume(key = ...)` a restart, a re-fork and a `supervise` re-run
all resume, delivering what arrived while it was down; with `fresh()` every activation re-primes and
that downtime is skipped.

There is no built-in retry: a failing @fetch@ or @deliver_to@ propagates and ends the subscription, and
resilience is composed at the call site — `supervise.forever` plus a converter turning the transient
failures (and, for an OAuth source, `auth_error`) into `supervise.interrupted`. The first poll is one
@schedule@ occurrence in, and under `seen_set` + `skip_backlog` that first poll is the priming one, so
the earliest notification such a subscription produces is two occurrences after it starts.
declarations.name: subscribe

declarations.documentation:
Spawn @task@ as a fiber in @nursery@, applied to @argument@ — the whole argument record of the call the fiber will make — and return immediately with a `fiber[Scope]` handle (identity only; `fiber_id` reads the id `cancel_by_id` addresses). A fork is a deferred call, so `region.fork(nursery = box, task = deliver, argument = { source = "mail:core", hop = 1 })` runs `deliver(source = "mail:core", hop = 1)`; @task@ keeps its own parameter names, a nullary task is forked with `argument = {}`, and a wider record fits (parameter records are contravariant). @name@ is an optional opaque tag the runtime echoes back in `roster`, `crashed` and `failed`.

@task@ is `-> null`: a fiber carries no result, and everything it produces leaves through its escalations, which surface at `watch`. A `-> never` body — a watcher that runs until cancelled — fits by subtyping. Its effect fits under the ceiling `E`, except its throws: the task parameter's row is `E | prelude.throw[unknown]`, because an uncaught throw is trapped at `watch` and delivered as the typed `failed` event rather than crossing the region as a throw, so a throwing task forks under a throw-free ceiling.

A fork routes by the handle alone, so forking into another nursery's handle is cross-nursery mail. The forked closure's captured environment travels with it into an instance the sender does not own, so such a fork sends a named agent applied to plain data, which captures nothing; inline closures belong to forks into a nursery the caller owns. Forking into a settled nursery panics — delivery is at-most-once; fold the fork with `supervise.once` + `supervise.signal_panics` where a lost message must be noticed.

Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the `provide` that opened this nursery.

Re-emit the nursery's fibers' escalations into the enclosing program as the ceiling effect `E`, plus the runtime's own `crashed` and `failed` events. It returns `never` — it only ever raises — so a handler (or any row covering `E | crashed | failed`) wraps it, and that covers everything any fiber can surface. This is the one channel out of a fiber: a normal completion and a cancellation are silent, and the two endings a task cannot report itself arrive as typed events — a panic as `crashed`, an uncaught `prelude.throw` as `failed`.

An escalation raised before any `watch` is installed is held durably and re-emitted in arrival order the moment one registers, so a watch installed later receives every earlier escalation. `watch` re-emits every escalation concurrently and adds no serialization of its own; the serialization point is the receiving handler, so two escalations to different handlers run concurrently, two to the same stateful (`var`) handler run one at a time in arrival order, and two to the same `parallel handler` run concurrently. One watch interleaves every fiber's stream, so a second adds no concurrency.

handler calls it in its own body, so two exclusives of one domain run one at a time, including against
a `parallel for` tool batch. Writes are last-write-wins, so this is what makes a read-modify-write
atomic.

Two consequences of the geometry. It binds to the nearest enclosing `workspace`, so an inner domain
shadows an outer one. And because prefix and domain are one install, the task runs inside the prefix of
the workspace serving it: a section that opens a workspace of its own descends further, and repeating
the directory it already stands in spells `app/memory/memory/...`. One lane per workspace, so a section
excludes the other sections of this workspace and interleaves with every other lane's.

The row is fixed to the store operations — everything else is computed before entering and closed over
— so a section never blocks on a model or a network. The answer crosses back as `unknown`; narrow it
with a `match` or `json.validate[T]`. With no workspace installed above the perform, the runtime serves
it at the project root, in one durable, project-wide FIFO across every run.

prefixed key, and a `list` gets @path@ prepended to its own path parameter, so nested workspaces
accumulate prefixes and the outermost bare perform is project-root
access) and the domain (one sequential handler serves `exclusive` by calling the section in its own
body, so its FIFO applies critical sections one at a time). The prefix handlers sit outside the domain,
which is what makes a section's keys resolve through the workspace it was opened in.

not — an empty segment, a `..`, an unchecked name — panics here rather than opening a workspace
elsewhere. `safe_segment` is the check for a name that came from outside the program.

The row is coarser than the truth, which shows in the escalation report: all five clauses are installed
and each re-performs its own operation, so this agent's row names all four store operations whatever
the continuation does. It reads as "reaches the store" rather than as the set of operations used.

is a `share` installed above the desks, so the desk's own workspaces do not travel with the task. It
lands in the shared place and opens whichever subdirectory it wants as its first move, which is what
lets one `share` serve every shared cell instead of one named request per cell. It binds to the nearest
enclosing `share`, so an inner shared place shadows an outer one.

The row is fixed to the store operations plus `exclusive`: a read-modify-write takes atomicity by
wrapping itself in `store.exclusive` inside the task, which lands in the shared place's own domain. The
answer crosses back as `unknown`; narrow it at the perform site. Unlike the four operations and
`exclusive`, this one is not runtime-served — with no `share` above it a `shared` rides to the run root
as an unanswered request rather than resolving to project-root keys, so the effect row is the guard.

Open the SHARED PLACE for the extent of @continuation@ — the bare `use store.share` form (the shared
place is where it is installed, exactly as a workspace is). It serves `shared` by calling its task in
the clause body, so a task runs here, under this site's workspaces and over this site's serial domain,
while the desks below go on opening their own workspaces and reaching nothing of each other's. The
clause is parallel, so `shared` itself serializes nothing — several desks' reads run at once, and
ordering is `exclusive`'s, taken inside the task.

The install order is the app's workspace, then `share`, then the desks. A task's row carries
`exclusive` and this provider re-performs it outward, so `share` sits inside a workspace for a shared
critical section to land in that workspace's domain; installed above one, `store.exclusive` surfaces in
the enclosing signature and those sections ride to the runtime's project-wide root FIFO. A second

shared place is expressed.

per cell. Where a boundary between shared cells is the semantics, a named request for that cell keeps
it; the two compose, since a named proxy installed below this one can perform `shared` in its own
clause.

declarations.documentation:
Call @deliver_to@ once per @schedule@ occurrence, forever, passing the occurrence's scheduled epoch
millisecond as @time@. It never resolves on its own (`-> never`) and runs until the run is cancelled;
@deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged.

The next occurrence is persisted and re-armed across a restart. If occurrences were missed while the
runtime was down, `watch` fires exactly once immediately on recovery (the earliest missed occurrence's
scheduled time — it does not backfill), then continues on schedule. Deliveries are serialized: the next
occurrence is not armed until the current delivery settles, so a slow @deliver_to@ rate-limits the ticks
rather than queueing them. There is no built-in retry: a @deliver_to@ that throws or panics propagates
and ends the watch, and resilience is composed at the call site with a `supervise` provider and a
converter.

declarations.documentation:
An offset east of UTC as its `±HH:MM` label, for a person reading it beside a civil time. UTC renders
`+00:00` rather than `Z` (`to_rfc3339` renders for the wire and spells it `Z`), and a non-whole-hour
offset renders faithfully (Asia/Kathmandu's 345 is `+05:45`).

declarations.documentation:
The instant's civil DATE at @offset_minutes@ (default UTC) as `YYYY-MM-DD` — the date half of
`to_rfc3339` without the clock, the zone or the `T`. ISO order is string order, so dates in this form
sort with `array.sort`, compare with `<`, and group by store-key prefix. A year outside 0..9999 renders
every digit rather than truncating, which keeps the date exact and drops the sort property.

declarations.documentation:
The instant as a wall clock reads it at @offset_minutes@ (default UTC) —
`2026-07-26 (Sun) 14:32 +09:00`: the civil date, the weekday, the time to the minute, and the offset,
in one line, so a reader needs no arithmetic. Seconds are absent; `to_rfc3339` is the render for a
machine reader.

declarations.documentation:
The offset of the IANA @zone@ in effect at @epoch_milliseconds@, in MINUTES EAST of UTC — exactly the
`offset_minutes` this module's agents take. Per-instant, so it is DST-correct by construction, and a
zone whose offset is not a whole hour answers it faithfully ("Asia/Kathmandu" is 345).

`null` when the runtime's zone database does not know @zone@. The names it does know are exactly the
ones a `cron` schedule's timezone accepts, being the same database: canonical IANA names, historical
aliases, any letter case, and the legacy abbreviations. An abbreviation names a whole zone with its DST
rules rather than the standard offset it resembles ("PST" answers -420 in July, not -480).

Deterministic in its arguments: it reads no clock, so a replay recomputes the same offset. The only
drift possible is a zone database update between executions. Pre-1900 instants round to the nearest
minute.
declarations.name: zone_offset

parameters.documentation: The instant to read the offset AT, in epoch milliseconds; fractions floor, like `to_civil`.
parameters.label: epoch_milliseconds

parameters.documentation: An IANA zone name (e.g. "Asia/Tokyo", "America/New_York", "UTC"); an unknown name answers null.
parameters.label: zone

epoch_milliseconds.description: The instant to read the offset AT, in epoch milliseconds; fractions floor, like `to_civil`.

zone.description: An IANA zone name (e.g. "Asia/Tokyo", "America/New_York", "UTC"); an unknown name answers null.

declarations.signature: primitive agent zone_offset(epoch_milliseconds: number, zone: string) -> integer | null

declarations.documentation:
Serve a fresh, unguessable public webhook URL for the extent of @subscriber@: the runtime converts
every POST to it into a call of @callback@ (JSON body in, JSON result out, status 200). @subscriber@
receives the URL, registers it wherever deliveries should come from, and stays alive while they flow;
when it returns the URL is deactivated and its result becomes `inbound`'s result. Both callables'
effects flow to the caller's handlers unchanged.

A body that does not conform to @callback@'s input schema is rejected 400 at the boundary and the
callback never runs. A callback that throws or panics on a well-formed delivery proxies up like any
escalation and cancels the whole endpoint; a handler around the callback's body turns that into a
per-request outcome. A delivery in flight across a runtime restart is lost (the provider's retry
redelivers); the URL itself is durable until @subscriber@ settles.
declarations.name: inbound

parameters.documentation: Called once per POST. A body failing its input schema is rejected 400 before it runs; its unhandled failure cancels the endpoint.
parameters.label: callback

parameters.documentation: The URL's owner: receives the minted public URL, and the endpoint serves exactly while it runs.
parameters.label: subscriber

declarations.signature: external agent inbound[R, effect E](callback: agent never -> unknown with E, subscriber: agent(url: string) -> R with E) -> R with E | io from "webhook"
